output.normalized_title: payment-processor: Redis memory usage > 98% with maxmemory-policy noeviction (payment-processor)
symptoms: Redis memory usage > 98% with maxmemory-policy noeviction

output.classification_reasoning: The primary symptom is Redis memory usage exceeding 98% with a maxmemory-policy set to noeviction, indicating that the in‑memory data store has exhausted its allocated storage capacity. This condition directly maps to a storage exhaustion failure. The impact is limited to the payment‑processor service, affecting 25 users and causing an 8‑minute outage, which suggests the issue is localized but requires coordination between the caching layer, the service configuration, and potential data eviction policies. Resolving it may involve scaling Redis, adjusting memory limits, or changing the eviction policy, tasks that are more involved than a simple configuration tweak but do not require a full architectural redesign, placing the operational effort at a moderate level of complexity.

prerequisites: Root access or AWS SSO role ProdOperations
Kubectl context set to production cluster
output.security_notes: Verify write freeze before any node reboot. Promote any read‑replica before terminating the primary instance.

recurring_patterns.symptom_pattern: Redis memory usage > 98% with maxmemory-policy noeviction

diagnostic_stage_assessment.notes: Current telemetry does not directly match any historical incident signatures or categories. Prior incidents involve storage exhaustion and database latency, not Redis memory pressure, indicating a potentially new failure mode.

output.governing_sla_rule: Minor disruption impacting < 100 users with standard SLA.
output.justification: The incident affects 25 users, well below the 100‑user threshold defined for a minor disruption. The outage duration is 8 minutes, which is within acceptable limits for Tier‑1 services under the standard SLA. Although the symptom (Redis memory usage > 98% with noeviction) is a new failure mode, the impact remains limited in scope and duration, matching the criteria for SEV-4 as per the governing rule.

remediation_steps.title: Validate Operator Access and Kubernetes Context
remediation_steps.description: Ensure the engineer has the required ProdOperations role (or AWS SSO) and that kubectl is pointed at the production cluster before any changes are made.
commands: aws sts get-caller-identity
kubectl config current-context
kubectl get nodes --selector=node-role.kubernetes.io/master
verification: AWS identity matches ProdOperations role
kubectl context name contains 'prod' or matches expected cluster identifier
Master nodes are reachable

remediation_steps.title: Assess Current Redis Memory State
remediation_steps.description: Collect detailed memory metrics from the Redis pod(s) to confirm the >98% usage and identify the largest keys or data structures.
commands: kubectl exec -n payment-processor -c redis $(kubectl get pod -n payment-processor -l app=redis -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- redis-cli INFO memory
kubectl exec -n payment-processor -c redis $(kubectl get pod -n payment-processor -l app=redis -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- redis-cli --bigkeys
verification: INFO memory shows used_memory_percent >= 98
BIGKEYS output lists top‑10 keys by size

remediation_steps.title: Mitigate Memory Pressure by Scaling Redis Replicas
remediation_steps.description: Add a read‑replica to off‑load traffic and increase total available memory. This is safe because the runbook notes to promote a read‑replica before terminating any primary.
commands: kubectl scale statefulset redis-primary -n payment-processor --replicas=2
kubectl get sts redis-primary -n payment-processor -o yaml | grep replicas
verification: New Redis pod reaches Ready status within 2 minutes
Metrics server shows combined memory usage < 80% across replicas

remediation_steps.title: Adjust Redis Eviction Policy and Maxmemory (Temporary)
remediation_steps.description: Switch the maxmemory‑policy from noeviction to volatile‑lru (or allkeys‑lru) and optionally raise maxmemory limit to give the system breathing room while a longer‑term solution is planned.
commands: kubectl exec -n payment-processor -c redis $(kubectl get pod -n payment-processor -l app=redis -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
kubectl exec -n payment-processor -c redis $(kubectl get pod -n payment-processor -l app=redis -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory 4gb
verification: CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy returns 'allkeys-lru'
CONFIG GET maxmemory returns the new value
Subsequent INFO memory shows used_memory_percent dropping below 85% within 5 minutes

remediation_steps.title: Post‑Remediation Health Validation
remediation_steps.description: Run application‑level health checks and confirm that payment processing latency and error rates have returned to baseline.
commands: curl -sSf https://payment-processor.internal/healthz
kubectl logs -n payment-processor deployment/payment-processor -c app --since=5m | grep -i error
kubectl top pod -n payment-processor | grep redis
verification: Health endpoint returns HTTP 200 with status OK
Error log count is zero or within normal threshold
Redis pod memory usage < 80%

rollback_plan.overall_strategy: Revert Redis configuration changes and scale back to the original replica count. All actions are idempotent and can be undone without data loss because Redis persistence (RDB/AOF) is enabled.

steps.description: Restore original maxmemory‑policy and maxmemory values.
commands: kubectl exec -n payment-processor -c redis $(kubectl get pod -n payment-processor -l app=redis -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy noeviction
kubectl exec -n payment-processor -c redis $(kubectl get pod -n payment-processor -l app=redis -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory 2gb
verification: CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy returns 'noeviction'
CONFIG GET maxmemory returns the original value

steps.description: Scale Redis StatefulSet back to the original replica count (single primary).
commands: kubectl scale statefulset redis-primary -n payment-processor --replicas=1
kubectl get sts redis-primary -n payment-processor -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'
verification: Only one Redis pod remains in Ready state
Application health checks remain OK after scaling down

steps.description: If any unexpected behavior persists, perform a rolling restart of the payment‑processor deployment to ensure it picks up the restored Redis settings.
commands: kubectl rollout restart deployment/payment-processor -n payment-processor
kubectl rollout status deployment/payment-processor -n payment-processor
verification: All payment‑processor pods report Ready=1/1
Health endpoint continues to return OK

prerequisite_checks: Operator credentials verified (ProdOperations role or equivalent)
Write‑freeze confirmed (no active deployments scheduled during remediation)
Current Redis persistence backups verified (RDB/AOF snapshot within last 15 min)
post_execution_checks: All verification checkpoints passed for each remediation step
No increase in user‑visible errors for payment‑processor service
